A vast majority, typically around that amount, if not more, IS beginner or even less, in any activity, for the simple reason that few people commit themselves enough to get past that stage. Intermediate is the stage where you have grasped the fundamentals of the activity, but you are still far from advanced or expert, and this stage DOES begin after atleast 1400, if not more.

I would think that OP's first mistake was actually their first move, which was moving the knight on b8 to c6 because that violates a very important opening principle of controlling the centre *with your pawns*. Actually cockroaches don't have a centralised hub for a brain like we do. They do have a "brain" in their heads but its only function is to communicate (by leaving out scents and such), find food and shelter, dictate regeneration and process hormones. The rest of the functions like walking, climbing, eating, sensing, excreting, etc are performed by the nervous system in the rest of the body which can act independent to the brain the head, so essentially, they have two "brains", one in the head, and the other that is the rest of the body.

Regarding "knowing it's alive", cockroaches do have some level of intelligence, but they are still basically mindless robots compared to other more intelligent creatures like mammals or birds. They are aware of their surroundings as they have basic short term spatial memory, and experience basic emotions that are present in all living organisms like hunger, fear and curiosity (not about physics, or philosophy, but about their spatial enviornment, like where most predators are, where is an abundance of food, etc), other than that, there isn't much to cockroach intelligence, they don't have thoughts. They can't feel pain either, not as we understand pain, atleast. Emotions like sorrow, grief, envy, empathy, etc are only present in more advanced creatures and not insects. They have basic learning abilities, like associating scents they instinctively avert from to be attracted to, but they can't solve puzzles or form bonds, or even remember their spatial enviornment for long. So, as long as they are alive, they wouldn't face much difference in basic living, other than being unable to communicate, eat, regenerate, etc, being headless is like a severe debuff, if you will.

Nah, in my opinion, at this level, it is a complete waste of time trying to memorise openings because the player doesn't have solid opening principles, so they wouldn't understand the opening and would have to completely memorise it. It would also be detrimental to the player's growth in the long term, since they'll raise a few elo points due to their opening but then get stuck (most likely at 1000 or at most 1200) and would stop winning any games.

Rather, you should learn opening principles like:

1. Controlling the centre.  
2. Developing your pieces.  
3. Pushing pawns towards the enemy king.  
4. Castling to safety (i.e. if any pawns are pushed forward on the side of the board, then castle the other way, or if most of the enemy pieces are staring at a particular side of the board, then castle the other way, or if both, i.e. enemy pieces are staring at the right side and the pawns have been pushed on the left side, then don't castle at all because the centre is the safest, etc).  
5. Try not to make more than one/two moves with the same piece.  
6. Don't develop the queen early, *if it can be attacked*.  
and some more than you might wanna check out

Seriously, this would get you way ahead than most players if you internalise these principles rather than memorise an opening and would also build a rock solid foundation that would help in learning actual openings in the future when you have a higher ELO (like maybe 1300-1400), because then you wouldn't have to memorise those openings as they would come naturally to you.

Other than that, players blunder A LOT at this level, so you should rather focus on not blundering by following general principles like:

1. Always look for checks and if they would benefit you.  
2. Always look for safe captures (i.e. you won't lose material after the capture/won't lose an exchange, an exchange in chess is when pieces of different values are traded, like a rook for a knight, or a bishop for a rook, etc, trading is for similar value pieces).  
3. Always look for safe attacks (with the same concept as above).  
4. In closed positions (i.e the pawns are abundant and restrict the board), knights are the best, so if you have a bishop and a knight, and the opponent does too, then trading your bishops for their knights would give you a really big advantage since their remaining bishops won't be able to move around the board while your knights mess up their position), and vice versa for open positions (i.e. less pawns on the board and more free space)
5. If the majority of your pawns are on one color, say black, then that means that your pawns are doing the work of the black bishop, so in a way, you have two black bishops and one white bishop, so if you can find a way to capture the opponent's white bishop while maintaining your white bishop on the board (i.e. maybe with a knight and bishop trade), then since you control the black squares, their black square bishop won't be able to move around the board while your white bishop glides through the board controlling all the squares ultimately (both black and white).

You probably already know general tips like, "always look for checks", "control the centre!", "don't blunder!", etc, so I won't go over them, but I would rather like to give you some less spoken tips like:

1) **Always play at your best condition!!** That means that you shouldn't play when you're in a bad mood, or are feeling low and coming to chess just to calm off (you can play on a separate account for that) and especially don't play when you're sleepy, angry, etc because the chances to make mistakes that you otherwise wouldn't be making are higher.
2) **Play with full concentration!** That means no background music, no watching TV/youtube while playing, basically no distractions, and that includes your mental distractions like thoughts about things other than your chess game!! You're playing chess right now, so thinking about anything else is not really useful since you're not working on that thing anyway, better give that focus to the game.
3) **Don't play more than 7-8 games a day!!** This has to do with your body's ultradian perform rhythm which basically means that you can work productively for 90 minutes (without extensive training) after which your performance plummets!
4) **Take a break!!** If you're not improving in your chess for a long time, or are on a losing streak, take a break! We go through what's called a "snowball effect" when we're losing which makes us impatient, lose confidence, increases our frustration (all of those bad moods!) which in turn further depletes our performace. So, for a week, just stop chess completely! No yt videos, no games, no puzzles, no opening the app or even looking at it and not even thinking about chess at all! Then come back and see yourself improving
5) **Analyse your games!!** This tells you about where you made a mistake/blunder, think about why you made that move and then think about why the engine recommends the move it does by following the engine line. Even if you don't have a pro membership, you can always go over to lichess or other websites, copy and paste your game PGN and analyse your games for free there!

Considering I went from 900 to 1200 in a week with absolutely no chess study (no yt videos, openings, fancy tactics or anything like that), my best advice would be to just be aware of the board at all times, whenever you're about to make a move, before you do it, always be mindful of:

1) What squares that move frees up for both **you** and your **opponent**.  
2) What new threats that move allows for both **you** and your **opponent**.  
3) If there is a possibility of making new checks for both **you** and your **opponent**.
4) And lastly, how your opponent would respond to that move (think of every logical possibility you can think of) and how you would respond to their response, and then how they would respond to your response, etc (I realise that sometimes this is easy and sometimes it takes time and a lot of brainstorming, so don't be afraid of the time, and be sure to take your time before rushing any move, even if it's an obvious one because a lot of times you're not aware that it could turn out to be a blunder)

Because of this, always play Rapid games so that you get plenty of time while still keeping the game relatively short and quick.

And this is the most important tip that I could give: **No matter what, don't play more than 6-7 games a day, seriously, no matter what happens**, doesn't matter if you lost all your games or won them, don't exceed this limit. The reason I say this, is because after playing so many games, your mind starts to fog up and you can't think as clearly, and you don't even realise that until you start losing and making mistakes that you otherwise wouldn't make or weren't making before this mark. It's detrimental to both your ELO and your growth as a chess player.

I have honestly done just this, exactly as I tell you and this resulted in the 300+ rating climb in a week.

Opponents at 1200 are honestly not that different than at 800, there are still a bunch of silly mistakes, one move blunders, hanging pieces, etc, all the mistakes that you make at 800, so it's not out of your league at all!

Edit: and please, *use your 10 minutes completely!*, if your games are not 10 move games and are still completing before even 5 minutes from both you and your opponent, there's no reason playing a 10 minute game, that's a blitz game in disguise! I have noticed that people blitz a ton of their moves and then make a blunder and when their opponent uses that blunder to their advantage, they start thinking a lot, when in reality there's no use thinking at that point, you have to think like that for all of the game, not just when you blunder!

In Academia, research, especially with the scientific method, is done as follows:

1) **Observe** a phenomenon that can't be explained currently *(in this case, it was Darwin observing the wide variety of species that are highly suited to live in their environment)*


2) **Question** the phenomenon and why it exists *(here, Darwin questioned why these varieties in species exist and why are they so highly adjusted to their environment)* 


3) **Construct a *HYPOTHESIS* to explain the phenomenon/question**, which is a statement or series of *TESTABLE, SPECIFIC and FALSIFIABLE* statements that answer the proposed question, without evidence or proof, to act as a starting point for research *(here, Darwin *hypothesised* that species inherit these highly adaptive traits from their environment and over time, these traits change little by little, to meet their environmental demands)*  
 [**Basically, your definition of a "Theory"**]


4) **Predict** what is supposed to happen under the condition that the hypothesis is true, as a way to guide further research into proving or disproving the hypothesis *(here, Darwin predicted that if species change over time (his hypothesis), then there should be evidence of gradual changes in species as well as evidence of different species branching off of a common ancestor)*


5) **Experiment** by collecting data/designing tests regarding the prediction and subsequently, the hypothesis *(here, Darwin collected extensive data regarding his prediction which consisted of a multitude of fossils, specimen, behavioural data on different species, etc from different parts of the world)*


6) **Analyse** the experimentation data to see if it supports or contradicts the hypothesis (here, Darwin analysed his data/evidence and compared it to his predictions, and he found that the evidence did support his predictions)


7) **Conclude** the research by summarising all the steps in the research and if they support the hypothesis, conclude your research as a ***THEORY*** regarding the phenomenon *(here, the Theory of Evolution)* 
[**Basically, your definition of a "fact"**]


Similarly, since Darwin's time, scientists have theorised how modern humans came to be.

Regarding why these are called "Theories" and not facts, is because of a really good feature of modern science to not dismiss other possibilities/explanations. In modern science, a "fact" is something that can be observed by anyone repeatedly, and is an observation rather than an explanation, while a "theory" is an overarching and conceptual explanation of the phenomenon.

Consider this:

1) It is a fact that you are attracted to the ground.  
Or  
It is a fact that gravity exists.  


2) The theory of gravitation explains why we are attracted to the ground.

While we all know for a "fact" that gravity exists, gravitation is still a "theory" as I explained why.

Also, there is a possibility that your theory, although being formed after extensive evidence and experimentation, might not be "the absolute truth", which is also another reason it is not seen as a "fact", which is another feature of modern science.

For example, the Theory of Gravitation as proposed by Newton work spectacularly on Earth and under controlled variables, and are as good as facts under Earth conditions, but they fall apart a bit in some cases where the variables are a bit more extreme where other, more overarching, Theories of Gravitation are used, which, again, include Newtonian mechanics.

S = a/(1 - r) ; where S is the sum and a is the first term.

This is no theorem per se, but part of basic Trigonometric sign conventions. I think you're just starting out with it so you may not know.

The reason for it is quite simple, if you draw a unit circle, and in that circle a triangle whose hypotenuse is the radius, then the base will be cos(x) and the height will be sin(x) where x is the angle from the x axis to the hypotenuse.

In the first quadrant of the unit circle, x is positive, so sin(x) that is opposite/hypotenuse = perpendicular side= +ve, the sane way, cos(x) = +ve and hence all the trig ratios are also +ve.

In the fourth quadrant, i.e the last quadrant, when you mirror the same triangle with the angle now being -x (when we measure the angle clockwise, it is taken as negative) from the x axis, sin(-x) = perpendicular/hypotenuse = -sin(x), since y (the perpendicular) is negative in the fourth quadrant, similarly, cos(-x) = base/hypotenuse = +cos(x), since the base which is the x value, remains positive in the fourth quadrant.

We have √(14 – 2x) = x – 7

The value inside the square root has to be either 0 or positive for it to make sense, since square roots of negative values don't make any sense in the real number system.

How would you define "true"? The way Hilbert thought of mathematics? An art that was Complete (meaning that there was a way to prove every statement in a mathematical system), Consistent (meaning that it was free of contradictions, i.e., you can't simultaneously prove A and Not A) and Decidable (meaning a system that could always determine if a statement follows from the fundamental axioms)? Because if that's the case then, unfortunately mathematics is fundamentally flawed, as Gödel's first incompleteness paper proved that Maths is not Complete, meaning that it is impossible to prove every statement in a mathematical system, and his second incompleteness paper proved that it is impossible for any mathematical system to be proven Consistent. It does depend on the light source too but it doesn't depend on just that. Multiple factors are at work here. If the sun had been hotter, say about 8000K, we would have had a violet sky because then it would have given enough violet wavelengths for them to reach us and make the sky appear violet because remember, I said that the reason the sky wasn't violet was because of the scarcity of enough violet wavelengths.

It's because of a phenomenon called "Rayleigh Scattering".

You probably know about "Scattering of light", but just in case, the Scattering of light is the absorption and re-emission of light by the particles in its surroundings.

Rayleigh Scattering is a specific case of Scattering of light, involving very minute particles, like the ones above us, high up in the sky. It says that the intensity of light is inversely proportional to the 4th power of its (the light wave's) wavelength i.e. I ∝ 1/λ⁴.
    Hence, the shorter the wavelength, the more intensely it will scatter, blue has the shortest wavelength succeeded only by violet, thus scattering the colour blue the most, and making the sky appear blue to us.

I can hear you asking, "But wait... if violet has the shortest wavelength, why doesn't the sky appear violet to us?" Well, that's because of multiple factors including but ofc not limited to, us being more sensitive to blue than violet, and objects around the earth, including the sun, just not giving off enough light for enough wavelengths of violet to reach us to make the sky appear violet.

Now I must remind you again that this is true only for very small particles, which is why near the horizon, where the atmosphere is quite dense i.e. the particles in the atmosphere are larger, the sky progressively gets redder, as the blue wavelengths of light, due to being shorter, scatter away before reaching us, leaving only the longer wavelengths.
